lines: 104 files do not match what this source builds:
... 92 further files not shown, use make build-verify ARGS="--top=0"

Both builds of the source in this checkout, in two different directories, wrote those bytes the same way, so the difference is not a toolchain that fails to reproduce itself: what is in the checkout was built from something else.
A build, and a commit of what it writes, brings the two back together.
160 files are in js/ and css/ that the build does not produce:
... 148 further files not shown, use make build-verify ARGS="--top=0"

A file no build writes any more, and that nothing in the source imports or names, is the remains of an earlier build or of something the app no longer uses. It still ships, it is loaded by nothing this source refers to, and it holds whatever it held when it was last written.
Only removing it from git removes it from a release.
The build produces 160 files that js/ and css/ does not hold:
... 148 further files not shown, use make build-verify ARGS="--top=0"
They belong to the output and are not committed, so a release built out of git alone is missing them, and whatever loads them is broken in it.
A build, and a commit of what it writes, brings the two back together.
140 files differ in what the build writes about itself only: the content hashes in the file names it refers to; the hashed file name a source map belongs to.
Their content is what this source builds, so nothing follows for the code. A hashed name changes with every build that changes the file it names, which is what the hash is there for.
83 committed files in js/ and css/ are source, not build output, and left out of the comparison:
js/text-files.mjs: named in lib/Listeners/FilesLoadAdditionalScriptsListener.php, and left as it is by the build
js/text-public.mjs: named in lib/Listeners/FilesSharingLoadAdditionalScriptsListener.php, and left as it is by the build
... 71 further files not shown, use make build-verify ARGS="--top=0"

The build reads what the source imports, so those files stay in the rebuilt tree. A file the app names in PHP, a template or info.xml, or in a script by its full path, is loaded by that name, and so is what it imports. Where no build writes other bytes under such a name, the file is a hand-written script, stylesheet or asset.
524 tracked files have uncommitted changes, and the rebuild used the working tree as it is, not the last commit.
So this says whether the output matches the source you are looking at, which is what a build would do. Against HEAD the answer can be another one.
npm ci and npm run build succeed on the tracked files alone, twice, in 122.4 s.
Nothing else was in the tree, which is the state a fresh clone and CI build in, so a build that needs a leftover from an earlier one would have failed here.
